reader.title: Lynching of Sandy King
bases: Both papers report men accused of cattle theft or rustling hanged by citizens without trial at or near Shakespeare, the Headlight calling it execution 'by Judge Lynch' (A1, A2).

The Epitaph says 'the citizens' disarmed a party of five armed rustlers and 'hung them all', and the Headlight says King was 'executed by Judge Lynch' as one of several cattle thieves; no lawful authority is reported (A1, A2). The size of the group of citizens is not stated, but disarming five armed men implies more than two.

Two independent reports, a Deming Headlight item (A1) and a Galeyville report to the Epitaph (A2), agree that accused cattle thieves or rustlers were lynched at Shakespeare, though they differ on names and number and A2 is second-hand.

summary.text: The lynching of Sandy King was the hanging of "Sandy" King and other men described as cattle thieves or "rustlers" by citizens at or near Shakespeare in late 1881, reported in mid-December of that year.
The Tombstone Epitaph, relaying a report current in Galeyville, said five rustlers were hanged after refusing a Grant county deputy sheriff's order to lay down their arms.
The Deming Headlight named King as one of those "executed by Judge Lynch."
The Deming Headlight called King "somewhat of a noted character" who might have "budded into a blooning desperado" had he lived.
The paper accused him of stopping "old man Heeman" near Sholdiers Holes some months earlier, taking his horse and firing a shot that grazed the old man's head.
His "last exploit," it said, came at Lordsburg, where he tried to take a bill of goods from a store at pistol point and a clerk shot him through the neck.
A traveler from Galeyville told the Epitaph it was "current and universally believed" there that five rustlers had been hanged near Shakspeare "last week."
In this version the men "came in to take the town," refused the deputy sheriff's order to disarm, and were disarmed and hanged by citizens who "came to the rescue."

The Headlight wrote that King's neck wound healed "just in time for the necktie matinee" at which he "played as end man," implying that others were hanged with him; neither paper says where, when, or by how many.
No report of an inquest, arrests or official inquiry appears in the coverage, and the Epitaph said the names of the victims "could not be learned."

The Lyon County Times of Silver City, Nevada, reprinted the Headlight piece on December 17 under the heading "'Sandy' King," recounting his alleged robberies and describing the hanging in stage slang.
The Epitaph ran its item on December 19 as "Lynching of Five Rustlers at Shakspeare," saying the men had "turned up their toes to the daisies" and adding no comment on the hanging itself.
Neither paper mentioned the race of King or the other men, and neither criticized the lynching.
The two accounts differ in detail: the Epitaph gave five victims but no names, while the Headlight named only King and gave no number.
The Headlight item was already in print in Nevada on December 17 and called the hanging recent, whereas the Epitaph's informant placed it in the week before December 19.

accounts.label: Deming Headlight
accounts.gist: King, a would-be 'desperado' with a record of armed robbery, was one of the cattle thieves recently executed by Judge Lynch at Shakespeare.

accounts.label: Galeyville report to the Epitaph
accounts.gist: Five rustlers came in to take the town, refused a Grant county deputy sheriff's order to disarm, and were disarmed and hanged by the citizens; names and particulars unknown.

framing.detail: The Headlight, reprinted under '"Sandy" King', presents the victim as a budding 'desperado' and the hanging as a 'necktie matinee' at which he 'played as end man'.
The Epitaph headed it 'Lynching of Five Rustlers at Shakspeare' and wrote that the men 'turned up their toes to the daisies', relaying the report without comment.

conflicts.note: The accounts are compatible on the core event; only the Epitaph gives a number, and its report is second-hand.
